section.title: Isaac Born, Hagar Sent
section.sectionRationale: After twenty-five years of waiting, the promise arrives: Sarah bears Isaac, the son of laughter, exactly as God had said. But the joy is soon crossed by conflict, as Ishmael is sent away. The chapter shows God keeping His word to the letter and caring even for the son who is not the heir.
section.thesis: God visits Sarah and does exactly what He promised, turning barren laughter into joy; yet the arrival of the son of promise forces a painful separation, in which God both narrows the line to Isaac and hears the cry of Hagar and Ishmael in the desert.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the birth of Isaac and Sarah's laughter of joy; the conflict that leads to Hagar and Ishmael being sent away; and God's provision for the boy in the wilderness.

verses.text: Now the LORD {{paqad|attended}} to Sarah as He had said, and the LORD did for Sarah what He had promised.
So Sarah conceived and bore a son to Abraham in his old age, at the very time God had promised.
And Abraham gave the name Isaac to the son Sarah bore to him.
When his son Isaac was eight days old, Abraham circumcised him, as God had commanded him.
Abraham was a hundred years old when his son Isaac was born to him.
Then Sarah said, “God has made me {{tsachaq|laugh}}, and everyone who hears of this will laugh with me.”
She added, “Who would have told Abraham that Sarah would nurse children? Yet I have borne him a son in his old age.”
So the child grew and was weaned, and Abraham held a great feast on the day Isaac was weaned.
But Sarah saw that the son whom Hagar the Egyptian had borne to Abraham was mocking her son,
and she said to Abraham, “Expel the slave woman and her son, for the slave woman’s son will never share in the inheritance with my son Isaac!”
Now this matter distressed Abraham greatly because it concerned his son Ishmael.
But God said to Abraham, “Do not be distressed about the boy and your maidservant. Listen to everything that Sarah tells you, for through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned.
But I will also make a nation of the slave woman’s son, because he is your offspring.”
Early in the morning, Abraham got up, took bread and a skin of water, put them on Hagar’s shoulders, and sent her away with the boy. She left and wandered in the Wilderness of Beersheba.
When the water in the skin was gone, she left the boy under one of the bushes.
Then she went off and sat down nearby, about a bowshot away, for she said, “I cannot bear to watch the boy die!” And as she sat nearby, she lifted up her voice and wept.
Then God {{shama|heard}} the voice of the boy, and the angel of God called to Hagar from heaven, “What is wrong, Hagar? Do not be afraid, for God has heard the voice of the boy where he lies.
Get up, lift up the boy, and take him by the hand, for I will make him into a great nation.”
Then God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water. So she went and filled the skin with water and gave the boy a drink.
And God was with the boy, and he grew up and settled in the wilderness and became a great archer.
And while he was dwelling in the Wilderness of Paran, his mother got a wife for him from the land of Egypt.

paqad.gloss: To visit, attend to, take note of and act. When God attends to Sarah, it means He turns His active care toward her to fulfill His word. The same verb marks moments when God intervenes to keep His promises, here bringing life to a barren womb at the appointed time.

tsachaq.gloss: To laugh. The name Isaac, Yitschaq, means he laughs, and this root has run through the story: Abraham laughed, Sarah laughed in doubt, and now she laughs for joy. God turns the laughter of unbelief into the laughter of praise, and invites all who hear to laugh with her.

shama.gloss: To hear, listen, heed. God heard the voice of the boy, echoing the meaning of Ishmael, God hears. The word ties this rescue to the earlier promise in chapter 16, showing that the God who hears the afflicted keeps hearing, even the outsider He did not choose as the covenant heir.

basic.context: After twenty-five years, God gives Abraham and Sarah the promised son, Isaac, exactly when He said. Joy soon meets conflict when Ishmael mocks and Sarah demands he be sent away. The key question is how God can be faithful to the child of promise and still care for the son who is not the heir.
basic.hermeneutics: This is history that fulfills a long-standing promise, and the point is God's exact faithfulness. The sending away of Hagar is painful, and the text names Abraham's distress, but God directs and comforts. Readers debate the harshness of the expulsion, yet God's care for the boy is unmistakable.
basic.originalLanguages: The chapter opens with God attending to Sarah, a word for God stepping in to act on His promise. Isaac's name means he laughs, and the laughter of doubt now becomes laughter of joy. In the desert God hears the boy, echoing the name Ishmael, which means God hears.
basic.typology: Isaac, the child of promise born by God's power to the as-good-as-dead, points to the miracle of grace and to the true Son. Paul reads Isaac and Ishmael as children of promise and of flesh, a picture of the two covenants.
basic.christ: Isaac, the long-awaited son who brings laughter and is born against all natural hope, foreshadows Christ, the promised Son through whom joy comes to the world. Paul says believers, like Isaac, are children of promise, born of the Spirit.
basic.god: God is faithful to the letter of His word, doing exactly what He promised at the very time He named. He is also compassionate, hearing the cry of an outcast boy and providing water and a future.
basic.crossReferences: Galatians 4 reads Isaac and Ishmael as two covenants. Romans 9 says through Isaac the offspring is reckoned. Hebrews 11 recalls the faith that received the promised son.
basic.oneStory: The son of promise finally arrives, proof that God keeps His word against every impossibility, and the line narrows to Isaac. Yet God still hears the outsider. The story presses on toward Christ, the ultimate promised Son, in whom the children of promise are born and the nations are blessed.

context.literary:
After chapters of delay, the birth itself is told in two verses, and the narrator spends those verses insisting on one thing. 'As He had said,' 'what He had promised,' 'at the very time God had promised,' verses 1 and 2. Three times in a row the event is tied back to God's word. The story is not mainly about a baby but about a promise kept to the letter, down to the date fixed in Genesis 17:21 and 18:14.

Laughter is the thread that ties the chapter together. Abraham laughed at the promise, Genesis 17:17, and Sarah laughed behind the tent, Genesis 18:12. Now the child is named Isaac, 'he laughs,' verse 3, and Sarah turns the word into praise, verse 6. Then, three verses later, the same root appears in the participle rendered 'mocking,' verse 9. Laughter that began in doubt and became joy now becomes the spark of conflict. The chapter moves from a feast, verse 8, to a mother sitting in the desert waiting for her son to die of thirst, verse 16.

The second half of the chapter echoes Genesis 16, where Hagar fled from Sarai into the desert, met the angel by a spring and learned that God hears. Now she is sent rather than running, and she is not told to go back but to go on. The same God meets her.

It also anticipates Genesis 22 so closely that the two chapters should be read together. In both, Abraham 'got up early' in the morning, 21:14 and 22:3, and sets out with one of his sons toward death. In both the boy is saved at the last moment when the angel calls 'from heaven,' 21:17 and 22:11. In both a parent's eyes are opened or lifted and a provision is seen, a well in 21:19, a ram in 22:13. Both end with a promise of a great posterity. Abraham loses both sons in a sense, and receives both back from God.

Note how the characters name Ishmael. Sarah calls him only 'the slave woman's son,' verse 10. God calls him 'the boy' and 'your offspring,' verses 12 and 13.
context.historical:
Abraham was a hundred years old, verse 5, and Sarah ninety, Genesis 17:17. Circumcision on the eighth day, verse 4, is the first time the rule of Genesis 17:12 is carried out on a newborn, marking Isaac as the covenant child from his first week.

Weaning came much later than in modern Western practice. Hannah kept Samuel at home until he was weaned and then brought him to Shiloh as a 'boy,' 1 Samuel 1:22-24, and two or three years seems a common span in the ancient world. A feast at weaning, verse 8, celebrated a child's survival through the dangerous early years. Since Ishmael was thirteen when he was circumcised, Genesis 17:25, a year before Isaac was born, he was probably around sixteen at this point. That makes his behaviour in verse 9 the act of a young man, and it means the 'boy' of verses 14 to 20 is a teenager, weakened by thirst.

Sarah's demand concerns inheritance, verse 10. Hagar had been given to Abraham as a wife, Genesis 16:3, and her son was Abraham's firstborn. Ancient law codes dealt with this very situation. At least one Mesopotamian code provides that if a father frees a slave woman and her children, they give up any share of the estate with the children of the principal wife. Sarah's 'expel,' then, may amount to a demand for exactly that: freedom for Hagar and Ishmael, and no claim on the inheritance. Israel's later law protected the rights of an unloved wife's firstborn, Deuteronomy 21:15-17, which makes it all the more notable that here God Himself directs the outcome, verse 12.

The geography is the southern desert. The Wilderness of Beersheba lies in the Negev. Paran, verse 21, is the wilderness south toward Sinai where Israel later camped, Numbers 10:12. Ishmael 'became a great archer,' verse 20, and archery remained a mark of his descendants; Isaiah 21:17 speaks of the 'archers, the warriors of Kedar,' Kedar being Ishmael's second son, Genesis 25:13. Hagar's choice of an Egyptian wife for him, verse 21, keeps him tied to her own homeland.
context.canonical:
The verb for God's attending to Sarah, verse 1, becomes a thread through the rest of Scripture. Joseph's dying words promise that 'God will surely attend to you,' Genesis 50:25. At the burning bush the LORD says, 'I have surely attended to you,' Exodus 3:16, and when Israel hears that the LORD 'had attended to the Israelites' they bow and worship, Exodus 4:31. The same verb describes God visiting His people with bread in Ruth 1:6 and opening Hannah's womb in 1 Samuel 2:21. Zechariah takes it up at the dawn of the gospel: 'He has visited and redeemed His people,' Luke 1:68.

Sarah heads a line of barren women whose sons are gifts of God: Rebekah, Genesis 25:21, Rachel, Genesis 30:22, Hannah, and finally Elizabeth, Luke 1:7. Their joy is gathered up in Psalm 113:9, 'He settles the barren woman in her home as a joyful mother to her children,' and in Isaiah 54:1, 'Shout for joy, O barren woman,' which Paul quotes in Galatians 4:27.

The New Testament uses this chapter directly. Romans 9:7-9 quotes verse 12, 'Through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned,' to show that God's people are defined by promise, not by descent alone. Hebrews 11:18 quotes the same words to measure how much Abraham had at stake in Genesis 22. Galatians 4:21-31 reads the whole story as an illustration of two covenants, and quotes Sarah's words in verse 10 as 'Scripture,' Galatians 4:30.

Ishmael's story does not end here. God keeps His word to him as well: twelve princes, Genesis 25:16, as promised in Genesis 17:20. Isaac and Ishmael stand together to bury their father, Genesis 25:9. And Isaiah 60:7 pictures the flocks of Kedar and the rams of Nebaioth, Ishmael's sons, going up on God's altar 'with acceptance.'

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to know how their nation began: not by human strength or planning but by a miracle of God kept to the day. The first hearers were Isaac's descendants. Their very existence was proof that God does what He says, and the chapter invited them to join Sarah's laughter, verse 6, and to trust the same God with promises not yet fulfilled.

He also wanted them to understand why the line ran through Isaac and not Ishmael. The contrast with Genesis 16 is deliberate. Ishmael was the son of a plan, Sarai's plan to 'build a family' through her maidservant, Genesis 16:2. Isaac was the son of a promise, born when all planning had become impossible. The covenant people were to understand themselves as children of grace.

And he wanted them to see that election does not mean indifference. Israel lived alongside the Ishmaelite tribes of the southern deserts, sometimes as rivals, Psalm 83:6. The chapter insists that God heard Ishmael, was 'with the boy,' verse 20, and made him a nation 'because he is your offspring,' verse 13. Israel was not to despise the peoples God had also blessed.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records a family crisis without holding up any of its members as a model. Sarah's demand may come from jealousy as much as from concern for the promise, and the narrator does not praise her. Abraham's provision of bread and a single skin of water, verse 14, is strikingly meagre for a wealthy man. What turns the account is God's word to Abraham, verse 12, which endorses the outcome and gives its covenant reason while promising care for Ishmael.

This does not make the chapter a rule for families. Later law forbade a father to disinherit a firstborn out of favouritism, Deuteronomy 21:15-17, and the narrowing of the covenant line to Isaac was a unique step in the history of redemption. When Paul quotes 'Expel the slave woman,' Galatians 4:30, he applies it to a way of relating to God, reliance on the law for standing, not to how believers should treat people.

What does carry forward is the character of God. He keeps His word at the time He sets, He hears the cry of the abandoned, and He provides for those outside the centre of the story. Those lessons are commanded elsewhere and illustrated here.

debates.question: Was the sending away of Hagar and Ishmael just, given its harshness?

views.label: A God directed narrowing of the covenant line
views.case: God Himself tells Abraham to listen to Sarah, 'for through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned,' verse 12. The inheritance could not be divided if the promise was to run through one son. God also guarantees Ishmael's future, verses 13 and 18, so the separation serves the covenant purpose while providing for the boy.

views.label: A painful human failure God then redeems
views.case: The scene shows real harshness: a teenager and his mother sent into the desert with a single skin of water, and Abraham's grief is named, verse 11. Some stress that God's word to Abraham makes the best of a situation born of Sarah's jealousy and the earlier scheme of Genesis 16, rather than commending the expulsion itself.

debates.bearing: The two views are not far apart. The text holds together a sovereign choice and a human mess, and God is present in both, directing the line through Isaac while hearing and rescuing Ishmael. Election and compassion stand side by side.

debates.question: What was Ishmael doing in verse 9?

views.label: Mocking or taunting Isaac
views.case: The BSB reads 'mocking,' and Paul says 'the son born by the flesh persecuted the son born by the Spirit,' Galatians 4:29. On this view the older half brother ridiculed the child whose birth had displaced him, perhaps at the very feast of verse 8, and Sarah saw a threat to the heir.

views.label: Simply playing
views.case: The participle can mean to play or to laugh, and the Septuagint and Vulgate add 'with her son Isaac,' as the BSB footnote notes. On this reading there was nothing sinister in the act; Sarah's reaction reveals her own fear or jealousy at seeing the slave woman's son alongside hers.

views.label: Playing the part of Isaac
views.case: Because the verb is built on the same root as Isaac's name, some suggest a wordplay: Ishmael was 'Isaac-ing,' acting as though he were the son of laughter and the heir. Sarah's reply, that he 'will never share in the inheritance,' verse 10, would then answer exactly that claim.

debates.bearing: The narrator leaves the act unexplained and focuses on its effect: it forces the question of the inheritance. Paul's reading in Galatians 4:29 picks up the enmity that later history confirmed, and it fits the pattern Genesis traces between the chosen line and its brothers.

study.originalLanguages:
Beyond attending, laughter and hearing, a handful of words and constructions shape the chapter.

The phrase 'at the very time' in verse 2 translates lammo'ed, 'at the appointed time.' The noun mo'ed is the word God used in His promise, 'At the appointed time I will return,' Genesis 18:14, and 'at this time next year,' Genesis 17:21. It later becomes the word for Israel's 'appointed feasts,' Leviticus 23:2, the fixed times when Israel met with God. Isaac's birth is a divine appointment kept.

Sarah's cry in verse 6 is literally 'Laughter God has made for me,' with the noun tsechoq placed first for emphasis. Her next clause, 'everyone who hears will laugh with me,' uses a preposition that can mean either with me or at me; the ambiguity lets the reader hear both the joy of neighbours and the old embarrassment of a ninety year old mother, now overwhelmed by joy.

The participle rendered 'mocking' in verse 9, metsacheq, comes from the same root in an intensive stem. Its range in Genesis is wide. Lot's sons in law thought he was 'joking,' Genesis 19:14. Abimelech saw Isaac 'caressing' Rebekah, Genesis 26:8. Potiphar's wife accused Joseph of coming 'to make sport of us,' Genesis 39:14 and 39:17. At Sinai the people rose 'to indulge in revelry,' Exodus 32:6. Context must decide, which is why the verse is debated.

Sarah's word 'Expel,' verse 10, is garash, to drive out. It is the verb of Genesis 3:24, 'So He drove out the man,' and of Cain's lament, 'You have driven me from the face of the earth,' Genesis 4:14. It later describes God driving out the nations before Israel, and Pharaoh who 'will drive you out completely,' Exodus 11:1. Its passive participle names a divorced woman in Leviticus 21:7. Abraham's act in verse 14 is described with shalach, to send away, the verb Deuteronomy 24:1 uses when a man sends his wife from his house. The vocabulary is that of a marriage being dissolved.

The Hebrew shifts its word for Ishmael. Where the narrator speaks from Hagar's side, in verses 14 to 16, he is the yeled, the child, and she 'left,' literally threw or cast, him under a bush, verse 15, the verb used when Joseph's brothers 'threw him into the pit,' Genesis 37:24. When God speaks, in verses 17 to 20, he is the na'ar, the lad, a word used for young men. The mother sees a helpless child; God sees a young man with a future.

Two small links close the story. Hagar sits 'about a bowshot away,' verse 16, and the boy grows up to be 'a great archer,' verse 20; the bow that measured her despair becomes the sign of his survival. And 'God opened her eyes,' verse 19, uses paqach, the verb of Genesis 3:7, where opened eyes brought shame, and of 2 Kings 6:17, where Elisha's servant is shown the hills full of God's chariots. Here opened eyes see a well that was there all along.

typology.type: Isaac, the son born by promise at the appointed time
typology.fulfillment: Isaac was named by God before his conception, Genesis 17:19, born when nature had given up, circumcised on the eighth day, and greeted with laughter. Jesus is named by the angel 'before He had been conceived,' circumcised after eight days, Luke 2:21, born 'when the time had fully come,' Galatians 4:4, and announced as 'good news of great joy,' Luke 2:10. The escalation is great. Isaac came from an aged womb by God's power; Jesus from a virgin by the Holy Spirit. Isaac carried the promise; Jesus is the one in whom all God's promises are kept. Isaac was himself a sinner who needed the grace he pointed to.

typology.type: The two sons, of the slave woman and of the free woman
typology.fulfillment: Paul says the story serves as an illustration of two covenants, Galatians 4:24. The son born 'according to the flesh' stands for a relationship with God grounded in human effort; the son 'born through the promise' stands for those born of the Spirit. 'Now you, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise,' Galatians 4:28, children 'born not of blood, nor of the desire or will of man, but born of God,' John 1:13. The picture has limits Paul himself respects: Hagar and Ishmael as persons are not rejected by God in Genesis. God hears them, provides for them, and blesses Ishmael. The illustration concerns two ways of standing before God, not two kinds of people.

Sarah's joy, 'God has made me laugh,' is the first of many songs of barren women turned into mothers, and Isaiah turns it into a prophecy for the whole people of God: 'Shout for joy, O barren woman,' Isaiah 54:1. Paul quotes that verse of the church born through the gospel, Galatians 4:27. Elizabeth's neighbours 'rejoiced with her,' Luke 1:58, just as Sarah said all who heard would laugh with her. Jesus uses the same picture of His resurrection: the woman in labour 'forgets her anguish because of her joy,' John 16:21. The type falls short only in scale; Sarah's joy filled one tent, the gospel's fills the world.

typology.type: The well opened for the outcast in the wilderness
typology.fulfillment: God opened Hagar's eyes to water when she and her son had given up hope, outside the covenant household and far from Abraham's tents. Jesus meets another woman beyond the bounds of Israel's favour at a well and offers her 'living water,' water that 'will become in him a fount of water springing up to eternal life,' John 4:10 and 4:14. He calls, 'If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink,' John 7:37, and the Bible ends with the promise, 'To the thirsty I will give freely from the spring of the water of life,' Revelation 21:6. Hagar's well kept a boy alive for a season; Christ's water gives life that does not end.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first by the way God keeps His word. Everything in verses 1 and 2 turns on God doing 'as He had said.' The birth of Jesus is told the same way. Gabriel tells Mary that 'no word from God will ever fail,' Luke 1:37, an answer to the very question asked in Sarah's tent, 'Is anything too difficult for the LORD?' Genesis 18:14. Matthew repeatedly says that events happened 'to fulfill what the Lord had said.' The God who kept a date with Sarah kept a far larger appointment when 'the time had fully come,' Galatians 4:4.

It leads to Christ by the line it secures. 'Through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned,' verse 12. Paul presses the word reckoned, or called: God's people are counted by promise, Romans 9:7-8, and the promise itself comes to rest in one Seed, Galatians 3:16. Isaac is not the end of the line but the proof that it will continue, and that God alone will determine where it goes.

It leads to Christ in the pattern of joy and hostility. Isaac's birth brings laughter, and almost at once the son of promise is met with contempt. Paul notices the pattern and says, 'It is the same now,' Galatians 4:29. Jesus' birth brought great joy to shepherds and wise men, and within months a king sought His life, Matthew 2:13. The child of promise is always both a gift and a provocation.

It leads to Christ also in the way God treats the one outside the line. The chosen son stays in the tent, and yet God goes into the desert after the other son. Jesus did the same, going to a Samaritan woman at a well, John 4, and to a Canaanite mother pleading for her child, whose faith He praised, Matthew 15:28. The descendants of Ishmael are not forgotten. Isaiah foresaw the flocks of Kedar and Nebaioth accepted on God's altar, Isaiah 60:7, and at Pentecost 'Arabs' heard the apostles 'declaring the wonders of God' in their own tongue, Acts 2:11. Through Isaac's greater Son, the blessing reaches Ishmael's sons too.

A caution is needed. Isaac is not a divine child, and the chapter is not an allegory in which every detail stands for something about Jesus. Paul's reading in Galatians 4 is explicitly an illustration drawn from the story, and it rests on the plain sense: the promised son comes by God's power, not by human planning. That plain sense is exactly what the gospel says about Christ, and about every believer who is born 'of God,' John 1:13.
study.god:
The chapter shows a God whose words and deeds match exactly. The narrator's triple insistence in verses 1 and 2 is a statement about God's character: He is not approximately faithful. He named the season, Genesis 17:21, and He kept the season. Twenty five years of waiting did not mean that God had forgotten, only that He had fixed a time, and His people learn to wait for His appointed times.

He is the God who acts on the impossible. Paul describes Abraham acknowledging 'the decrepitness of his body' and 'the lifelessness of Sarah's womb,' Romans 4:19, and yet being 'fully persuaded that God was able to do what He had promised,' Romans 4:21. Isaac's birth is a small resurrection, life from a womb that was dead, and it prepares the way for Abraham's faith in Genesis 22 that God could raise the dead.

He gives joy. Sarah says, 'God has made me laugh,' verse 6. Joy is not only a human reaction to God's gifts; it is itself something God makes. The laugh that once doubted God is redeemed, not rebuked.

He is sovereign in choosing. God determines that the line runs through Isaac, verse 12, over Abraham's distress. His choice is not arbitrary, since it follows the promise He had made, but it is not up for negotiation.

And He is tender toward the one not chosen for the covenant line. He hears 'the voice of the boy,' verse 17, even though it is Hagar whose weeping is described in verse 16. The boy's own cry is not recorded, yet God hears it; the name Ishmael, God hears, is proved true again, as it was when God said 'As for Ishmael, I have heard you,' Genesis 17:20. God speaks gently: 'What is wrong, Hagar? Do not be afraid.' He does not create a new well; He opens her eyes to one already there, verse 19. And He stays: 'God was with the boy,' verse 20, the same assurance later given to Isaac, Genesis 26:24, and to Joseph, Genesis 39:2.

The chapter holds election and compassion together without explaining away either. God chooses Isaac; God blesses Ishmael. Readers who stress only the first make God cold, and readers who stress only the second make the promise vague. Scripture keeps both.

For worship, this invites trust in God's timing, joy that He Himself gives, and confidence that He hears those who can no longer find words, the lost, the thirsty, and those left under a bush in the desert.

crossReferences.note: God names Isaac before his conception, promises to establish the everlasting covenant with him, and sets the time: 'at this time next year.' In the same breath He promises that Ishmael will become a great nation with twelve rulers. Genesis 21 keeps both halves of that word.

Sarah laughs to herself at the promise, and the LORD asks, 'Is anything too difficult for the LORD?' fixing the appointed time. Her laughter in Genesis 21:6 is the answer to that question, doubt turned into praise at exactly the time God named.

The earlier desert scene. Hagar flees, the angel of the LORD finds her by a spring, gives her son the name Ishmael because 'the LORD has heard your cry,' and she names God the One who sees her. Genesis 21 repeats the pattern of hearing and seeing when she is sent away.

Paul tells believers that 'like Isaac' they are children of promise, notes that the son born by the flesh persecuted the son born by the Spirit, and quotes Genesis 21:10 as Scripture. The story becomes an illustration of freedom in Christ over slavery to the law.

Paul quotes Genesis 21:12, 'Through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned,' and Genesis 18:14 to show that God's word has not failed. Not all of Abraham's physical descendants are children of the promise; God's people are defined by His promise and call.

Sarah conceived by faith 'because she considered Him faithful who had promised,' and from one man 'as good as dead' came countless descendants. Hebrews reads the birth of Isaac as both God's miracle and the fruit of Sarah's trust.

The same verb used of the LORD attending to Sarah describes Him attending to Hannah, who then bore more children. Hannah, like Sarah, was a barren woman whose son was a turning point in Israel's story, and her song celebrates the God who reverses fortunes.

When Elizabeth, barren and old, gives birth to John, her neighbours hear of the Lord's mercy 'and they rejoiced with her.' The scene echoes Sarah's words that all who heard would laugh with her, as the gospel opens with another miraculous birth.

God's promise to Ishmael is fulfilled: twelve princes of their tribes, as promised in Genesis 17:20. The boy God heard under the bush becomes a nation, showing that God's word to those outside the covenant line is kept as carefully as His word to Isaac.

In Isaiah's vision of the nations streaming to Zion, the flocks of Kedar and the rams of Nebaioth, named after Ishmael's sons, go up on God's altar with acceptance. The descendants of the son sent away are gathered into the worship of the God who heard him.

'He settles the barren woman in her home as a joyful mother to her children.' The psalm turns Sarah's experience into a general praise of God, who lifts the lowly and whose greatness is seen in reversing hopeless situations.

Jesus offers a Samaritan woman water that will become 'a fount of water springing up to eternal life.' Like Hagar, she is an outsider at a well, and God's provision meets her where she did not expect to find it.

study.oneStory:
The whole story of redemption has been waiting on this birth. In Genesis 3:15 God promised a seed of the woman who would undo the serpent's work. In Genesis 12 He promised Abraham a great nation and blessing for all families of the earth. Everything hung on a son, and for twenty five years there was none. Abraham and Sarah even tried to secure the promise by their own means in Genesis 16. Genesis 21 answers all of this: the son arrives by God's power at God's time, and the story can go on.

The chapter also sets a pattern for the rest of the Bible. The line of promise narrows by God's choice: Isaac and not Ishmael, then Jacob and not Esau, then Judah and David. Each narrowing is painful, and each time God shows care for those outside the line. The narrowing is not the goal. It is the means by which the blessing will one day widen to all nations.

Israel's later history repeats the birth pattern again and again. When the nation seems dead in Egypt, God attends to them, Exodus 4:31. When Israel is barren and desolate in exile, Isaiah tells her to sing like a barren woman about to have more children than she can count, Isaiah 54:1. God keeps bringing life where there was none.

The story reaches its centre in Christ, the promised Son born when the time had fully come, in whom the offspring of Abraham is finally reckoned. Through Him the family of promise is opened to Jews and Gentiles alike, Galatians 3:29, including the descendants of Ishmael, who heard the gospel at Pentecost. Believers are now children of promise like Isaac, and the church sings the barren woman's song.

The new creation completes it. The thirsty will drink freely from the spring of the water of life, Revelation 21:6, and every tear will be wiped away, Revelation 21:4. The laughter of Sarah, the relief of Hagar at the well, and the joy of the neighbours who laughed along are small foretastes of the joy of the whole redeemed creation when God has kept every promise He has made.

quiz.q: How does the chapter emphasize God's faithfulness in Isaac's birth?

options.text: God did for Sarah exactly what He had promised, at the very time He had said.
options.note: The text stresses precise fulfillment of God's word.

options.text: Isaac was born much sooner than God had promised.
options.note: He was born at the appointed time, not sooner; the point is exactness.

options.text: Isaac was born through ordinary, natural circumstances.
options.note: The birth was a miracle to an aged, barren couple, not ordinary.

options.text: God's promise was only partly fulfilled.
options.note: The promise was fully and exactly kept.

quiz.q: What does the name Isaac mean, and how does it fit the story?

options.text: He laughs, gathering up the laughter of doubt now turned to joy.
options.note: Sarah says God has made her laugh, turning earlier doubt into praise.

options.text: God hears, marking that God heard Sarah's prayer.
options.note: That meaning belongs to Ishmael; Isaac means he laughs.

options.text: Father of many, celebrating Abraham's descendants.
options.note: That is the meaning of Abraham's name, not Isaac's.

options.text: God provides, recalling the gift of water.
options.note: Isaac means he laughs; provision is a theme, not the name's meaning.

quiz.q: How did God respond when Hagar and Ishmael were dying in the desert?

options.text: He heard the boy's voice, comforted Hagar, and provided a well of water.
options.note: God's hearing echoes the meaning of Ishmael's name.

options.text: He ignored them because Ishmael was not the heir.
options.note: God was not the covenant line through Ishmael, yet He heard and provided.

options.text: He sent them back to Abraham's household.
options.note: He provided for them in the wilderness rather than sending them back.

options.text: He let the boy die as judgment.
options.note: God saved the boy and promised to make him a nation.

quiz.q: Why did God tell Abraham to listen to Sarah about sending Ishmael away?

options.text: Because through Isaac his offspring would be reckoned, narrowing the covenant line.
options.note: God directs the line of promise through Isaac while still blessing Ishmael.

options.text: Because Ishmael had no future at all.
options.note: God promised to make Ishmael a great nation; he did have a future.

options.text: Because Abraham no longer cared about Ishmael.
options.note: The text says Abraham was greatly distressed over his son.

options.text: Because Sarah was acting against God's will.
options.note: God confirmed Sarah's word as serving His covenant purpose.

quiz.q: How does Paul use Isaac in the New Testament?

options.text: As the pattern of believers who are children of promise, born through the Spirit.
options.note: Galatians 4 makes Isaac a picture of the covenant of promise.

options.text: As an example of salvation earned by works.
options.note: Isaac pictures promise and grace, not works.

options.text: As a warning against having children in old age.
options.note: That misses Paul's allegory of the two covenants entirely.

options.text: As proof that the promise failed.
options.note: Isaac is proof the promise succeeded, born exactly as God said.

questions: God did exactly what He promised, at exactly the time He said, after twenty-five years. Where are you waiting on a promise of God, and how does Isaac's birth encourage you?
Sarah's laughter of doubt became laughter of joy. Has God ever turned something you doubted into a cause for praise?
God heard the cry of an outcast boy in the desert. Who are the overlooked people in your world whose cries God is calling you to notice?
The coming of the promised son brought both joy and painful conflict. How do you hold on to God's faithfulness when His blessings arrive tangled with hard circumstances?
Paul says believers are children of promise, like Isaac, born by the Spirit. How does it change your sense of identity to know you belong to God by promise, not by your own effort?

translationNotes.note: Attended to translates a verb meaning to visit or take note and act; it signals God's active intervention to keep His word to Sarah.
God has made me laugh plays on the name Isaac, he laughs; the same root has carried doubt and now carries joy.
Mocking may also be rendered playing or laughing; some manuscripts read mocking her son, and the word again echoes the laughter theme, here turned hostile.
